title: LLM application engineering: APIs, context, evals, production
summary: The most job-critical module for AI Engineer and FDE roles: reliable API engineering (structured outputs, retries, concurrency, fallbacks), prompt and context engineering, cost levers (caching, routing, batch), systematic evaluation (error analysis → golden sets → calibrated judges → CI) and production (tracing, cost/latency, guardrails). Spine: official provider docs + Hamel Husain/Shreya Shankar eval writing + Anthropic engineering posts + free DLAI short courses + rohitg00 Phase 11/17 builds. Needs only M03 and M09.U01–U03.

practice.title: ask.py — a disciplined CLI
practice.brief: Write ask.py that reads the key from env, pins a dated model ID, sends system + user messages, and appends one JSONL line per call: model, finish/stop reason, input/output tokens, computed cost, latency. It refuses to run when the counted prompt exceeds a budget. Run the same script against a hosted model and a local Ollama model through LiteLLM.
practice.done_when: JSONL log with ≥10 calls across two providers (one local), including one deliberately truncated call showing finish_reason/stop_reason = length/max_tokens, and one refused over-budget prompt.

quiz.prompt: finish_reason = 'length' (OpenAI) / stop_reason = 'max_tokens' (Anthropic) means:
options: The output hit the max-token limit and is probably truncated
quiz.explain: Treat it as an incomplete answer: raise the limit, shorten the task, or continue.

quiz.prompt: Pinning a dated model snapshot instead of an alias mainly protects against:
options: Silent behaviour changes when the alias is repointed
quiz.explain: Aliases move to newer snapshots; your evals only hold for the version you tested.

quiz.prompt: Which content belongs in the system prompt?
quiz.explain: User data and tool output arrive in user/tool turns; the system prompt sets durable behaviour.

quiz.prompt: Why log token usage per request from day one, even in a prototype?
rubric: Cost: usage is what you are billed on and the basis of any cost report
Debugging: unusually long inputs/outputs reveal prompt bloat or truncation
Baseline: later optimizations (caching, routing) need a before number

outcomes: You can retry 429/5xx with jittered exponential backoff and refuse to retry 4xx client errors.
You can run hundreds of calls concurrently with bounded parallelism and per-call timeouts.
You can stream tokens to a browser via SSE and fall back to a second model on repeated failure.

practice.title: 500 tasks, no drama
practice.brief: Process 500 short tasks with asyncio and a Semaphore(8). Add jittered backoff on 429/5xx, a per-call timeout, an idempotency key in logs, and fallback to a second model after 3 failures. Expose one endpoint that streams a response over Server-Sent Events with FastAPI. Report p50/p95 latency, retries, fallbacks and failures.
practice.done_when: A run report showing 500 completed tasks, counts of retries/fallbacks/failures, p50/p95 latency, and a curl or browser demo of the SSE stream.

quiz.prompt: Jitter is added to exponential backoff to:
options: Avoid synchronized retry storms from many clients
quiz.explain: Randomized delays spread retries out instead of all clients retrying at the same instant.

quiz.prompt: Streaming primarily improves:
options: Perceived latency (time to the first visible token)
quiz.explain: Total generation time is similar; users see output sooner.

quiz.prompt: A 400 'invalid request' error should usually be:
options: Sent to the fallback model forever
quiz.explain: Client errors are deterministic; retrying wastes quota.

quiz.prompt: When is retrying a tool-calling request unsafe, and how do you make it safe?
rubric: Unsafe when the tool has side effects (payment, email, DB write) that may have already happened
Fix: idempotency keys / dedup on the server side, or check state before re-executing
Separates retrying the model call from re-executing the tool

practice.title: Invoice/CV extractor, three ways
practice.brief: Define a Pydantic schema with enums, optional fields and a custom validator. On 50 documents compare (i) prompt-only JSON, (ii) native structured outputs, (iii) a validate→repair loop. Report schema-valid rate and field-level accuracy against your hand labels, and how a refusal is represented. Add one tool, lookup_currency_rate, via function calling, executed by your code.
practice.done_when: A results table (3 methods × valid rate × field accuracy), 50 hand labels committed, a refusal test case, and a passing test for the tool-call round trip.

quiz.prompt: Constrained decoding guarantees:
quiz.explain: It masks invalid tokens at each step; it cannot check whether values are true.

quiz.prompt: In function calling, who executes the function?
quiz.explain: The model emits a call with arguments; you run it and return the result.

quiz.prompt: A schema-valid extraction can still be wrong because:
options: The values may be hallucinated or misread
quiz.explain: Validity ≠ correctness; you still need field-level evals.

quiz.prompt: How should your service represent 'the model refused' differently from 'the model produced invalid JSON'?
rubric: Refusal is a distinct, expected outcome (e.g. refusal field/stop_reason) returned to the caller, not retried blindly
Invalid JSON is a parsing failure: retry/repair, then error
Both are logged and counted separately in evals

practice.title: Four-version prompt changelog + thinking budget
practice.brief: Take one classification task with 40 labelled items. Score 4 prompt versions (bare → constraints → delimited data with XML tags → 3 diverse examples) and keep a changelog of accuracy per version. Then run the best prompt on a reasoning model at two thinking/effort settings and compare accuracy, latency and cost.
practice.done_when: A changelog table with 4 prompt versions × accuracy, plus 2 reasoning settings × accuracy × p50 latency × cost per item.

quiz.prompt: Wrapping untrusted input in delimiters/XML tags mainly helps:
options: The model distinguish instructions from data
quiz.explain: Clear boundaries reduce the chance the model follows text inside the data as instructions (not a full injection defence).

quiz.prompt: Few-shot examples work best when they are:
options: Diverse and canonical for the expected behaviour
quiz.explain: Near-duplicates teach surface patterns; diverse examples show the decision boundary.

quiz.prompt: Raising a reasoning model's thinking budget typically trades:
options: More latency and cost for potentially higher accuracy on hard tasks
quiz.explain: Thinking tokens are billed and take time; gains concentrate on hard, multi-step problems.

quiz.prompt: Why can a prompt change that fixes one failure category make overall quality worse, and how do you detect it?
rubric: Explains interaction effects: new instructions shift behaviour on other cases (over-correction)
Detection: re-run the full labelled set, not just the failing examples; compare per-category
Mentions keeping a frozen regression set/changelog

practice.title: Needle test + compaction
practice.brief: Insert a fact at 5 positions in contexts of 2k/16k/64k tokens (with distractors) and plot accuracy by position and length for one model. Then implement compaction for a 40-turn support chat (summarize old turns, keep a structured facts block) and measure accuracy on 20 recall questions vs full history, plus token savings.
practice.done_when: A heat-map/plot of accuracy by position × length, and a table: full history vs compacted → accuracy on 20 questions and tokens per turn.

quiz.prompt: 'Context rot' refers to:
options: Declining recall/precision as more tokens are added to the context
quiz.explain: Even within the window, models use long contexts less reliably.

quiz.prompt: Compaction is:
options: Summarizing/condensing history to continue in a fresh context
quiz.explain: It keeps the important state while freeing the window.

quiz.prompt: 'Just-in-time' context means:
options: Keeping references and loading data via tools when needed
quiz.explain: Agents fetch files/records on demand instead of stuffing them in.

quiz.prompt: Give one case where stuffing a 200k-token window beats retrieval, and one where it doesn't.
rubric: Beats retrieval: a single bounded document needing global reasoning (e.g. one contract) that fits and is reused (cacheable)
Loses: large/changing corpora, needle facts, cost/latency-sensitive traffic, permission filtering
Mentions measuring both on the same eval

practice.title: Cheaper without getting worse
practice.brief: Move prompts to versioned files whose ID is logged on every call. Restructure a RAG prompt so instructions + tool definitions form a stable cacheable prefix; measure cached-token share and cost per request before/after. Build a 2-tier router (cheap model, escalate on low confidence or validation failure) and report cost and quality vs always-strong on your eval set. Push 200 offline items through a batch API.
practice.done_when: A before/after table (cached share, cost/request), a router table (cost, pass rate) vs always-strong, and a completed batch job with results joined back to inputs.

quiz.prompt: Prompt caching only helps when:
options: A long identical prefix is reused across requests
quiz.explain: Caches match on exact prefixes; anything variable must come after the cached part.

quiz.prompt: The main risk of semantic (embedding-similarity) caching is:
options: Returning a cached answer to a question that is similar but materially different
quiz.explain: 'Refund for order 123' and 'refund for order 124' embed almost identically.

quiz.prompt: Batch APIs are a good fit for:
options: Offline evals and backfills that tolerate hours of latency
quiz.explain: They trade latency (up to ~24h) for a large discount.

quiz.prompt: How would you prove your router saved money without lowering quality?
rubric: Same frozen eval set for router vs always-strong; report pass rate with confidence intervals
Cost per successful task, not just per call
Inspect escalation rate and failures of cheap-model answers that were not escalated

practice.title: 100 traces → failure taxonomy
practice.brief: Log 100 real or synthetic traces from your U03 extractor or a chatbot. Write a free-text note on every failure (open coding), cluster notes into 5–8 failure modes (axial coding) and count them. Pick the top 2 and write a binary pass/fail definition for each with 2 pass and 2 fail examples.
practice.done_when: A spreadsheet/CSV with 100 annotated traces, a frequency table of 5–8 failure modes, and two written pass/fail definitions with examples.

quiz.prompt: The recommended first step before choosing eval metrics is:
options: Read and annotate real traces to find failure modes
quiz.explain: Generic metrics measure things that may not be your failures.

quiz.prompt: Binary pass/fail criteria are often preferred over 1–5 scales because:
options: They are clearer, more consistent between raters, and actionable
quiz.explain: Likert midpoints are ambiguous and drift between raters.

quiz.prompt: Axial coding means:
options: Grouping open-coded notes into higher-level failure categories
quiz.explain: Open coding = free notes; axial coding = relating them into a taxonomy.

quiz.prompt: Your top failure mode is 'ignores the user's date format.' Write a precise pass/fail definition.
rubric: States the input condition (user specified a format explicitly or by example)
Pass = every date in the output uses that format; Fail = any date in another format
Covers edge cases: no dates in output, ambiguous formats

practice.title: 150-case golden set
practice.brief: Build 150 cases: 100 sampled from your U07 traces and 50 synthetic ones generated over explicit dimensions (persona × task × difficulty), each hand-verified. Write code-based assertions (regex, schema, numeric tolerance, forbidden phrases). Freeze a 30% held-out split you never tune on and add a contamination check (no held-out item appears in prompts/few-shot examples).
practice.done_when: golden.jsonl (150 rows with dimension tags), assertions passing in pytest, a frozen test split file with a hash recorded, and a contamination check script.

quiz.prompt: A held-out test split exists to:
options: Estimate quality on cases you did not tune prompts against
quiz.explain: Tuning on everything overfits your prompts to the eval.

quiz.prompt: Exact match is appropriate for:
quiz.explain: Exact match works when there is one correct normalized string.

quiz.prompt: Synthetic test generation is most useful when you:
options: Define dimensions to cover, then review samples
quiz.explain: Dimensions give coverage; review removes unrealistic or wrong cases.

quiz.prompt: How could your eval set become contaminated, and how would you detect it?
rubric: Cases copied into few-shot examples/prompts, or used for tuning; public benchmark items in model training data
Detection: string/embedding overlap checks between eval items and prompts/training data; suspiciously high held-out scores
Prevention: frozen hashed split, provenance per item

practice.title: Calibrated judge report
practice.brief: For one failure mode from U07, hand-label 80 outputs pass/fail. Write a judge prompt with a precise definition and examples. Split 40 dev / 40 test, iterate only on dev, then report TPR, TNR and raw agreement on test. For a pairwise version, swap A/B order on 30 pairs and report the position-bias rate.
practice.done_when: A report with confusion matrix on the 40 test items, TPR and TNR, the final judge prompt, and a position-swap consistency percentage.

quiz.prompt: A judge with 95% accuracy on a dataset where 95% of outputs pass may be useless because:
options: It may approve everything — check TNR on the failures
quiz.explain: On imbalanced data, measure TPR and TNR separately.

quiz.prompt: Position bias is tested by:
options: Swapping the order of A and B and checking consistency
quiz.explain: Zheng et al. found judges often prefer the first (or second) answer regardless of content.

quiz.prompt: You should iterate the judge prompt on:
options: A dev split, then report on an untouched test split
quiz.explain: Otherwise the reported agreement is overfit.

quiz.prompt: Why must a judge's criterion be one specific failure mode rather than 'overall quality'?
rubric: Specific criteria are measurable and calibratable against human labels
'Overall quality' mixes dimensions, drifts and gives non-actionable scores
Ties each judge to a failure mode from error analysis

practice.title: Eval gate in CI
practice.brief: Add a GitHub Actions workflow that runs your code checks plus the U09 judge on the frozen split whenever files in prompts/ or src/llm/ change. Fail the build when pass rate drops by more than an agreed margin (justify it with a confidence interval) and post a markdown diff of newly failing cases to the PR.
practice.done_when: A PR that intentionally degrades a prompt shows a failed check and a bot comment listing the newly failing cases; a passing PR shows green.

quiz.prompt: With 50 test cases at 90% pass rate, the 95% confidence interval is roughly:
options: ±8–10 points, so small regressions are undetectable
quiz.explain: Binomial SE = sqrt(0.9·0.1/50) ≈ 4.2 points; ×1.96 ≈ ±8.

quiz.prompt: CI evals should run on every PR that:
options: Changes prompts, models, retrieval or LLM code
quiz.explain: Path filters keep cost down while catching real regressions.

quiz.prompt: A useful regression report shows:
options: Per-case diffs of newly failing cases
quiz.explain: Means hide which behaviours broke.

quiz.prompt: How do you keep CI eval cost bounded as the suite grows?
rubric: Path filters / run only on relevant changes; cheap deterministic checks first, judge only where needed
Caching unchanged results, sampling a stratified subset on PRs and the full suite nightly
Batch APIs or cheaper judge models calibrated against the expensive one

practice.title: Every request is a trace
practice.brief: Instrument your app so every request yields a trace: spans for retrieval, each LLM call (model, tokens, cost, latency, prompt version) and tool calls, plus thumbs up/down feedback attached to the trace. Build a dashboard for p95 latency, cost/day and feedback rate. Run your U09 judge nightly on a 5% sample of traces. Redact phone numbers and CNICs before storage.
practice.done_when: A screenshot/link of a trace tree with all span types, a dashboard with the three metrics, a nightly judge job log, and a test proving PII is redacted in stored traces.

quiz.prompt: A trace differs from a log line in that it:
options: Links the nested spans of one request end to end
quiz.explain: Parent/child spans let you see where time, cost and errors occurred inside one request.

quiz.prompt: Online evaluation means:
quiz.explain: It catches drift and failure modes that never appeared offline.

quiz.prompt: Which should be redacted before storing traces?
options: PII such as phone numbers and CNIC numbers
quiz.explain: Traces often contain raw user input; storing PII creates legal and security risk.

quiz.prompt: Which three fields would you require on every LLM span, and why?
rubric: Model ID/version and prompt version (reproducibility, regressions)
Token usage + cost and latency (cost/latency engineering)
Trace/request/user or session ID and outcome/status (debugging, joining feedback)

quiz.prompt: Indirect prompt injection arrives via:

quiz.prompt: A guardrail with a high block rate but 15% false positives on benign traffic is:
options: Likely unusable without tuning — measure both sides
quiz.explain: Blocking one in seven legitimate users destroys the product.

quiz.prompt: The 'lethal trifecta' combines private data access, untrusted content, and:

quiz.prompt: Why can't a system prompt that says 'ignore instructions in documents' be your only injection defence?
rubric: Models follow instructions probabilistically; adversarial text can override system prompts
Defence in depth: least-privilege tools, removing an exfiltration path, output filtering, human approval
Must be tested with an adversarial set, not assumed
